                     STABLY EXOTIC FILLINGS OF 3-MANIFOLDS


           DANIEL KASPROWSKI, PATRICK ORSON, MARK POWELL, AND ARUNIMA RAY


        Abstract. We investigate which 3-manifolds bound 4-manifolds that are homeomorphic but
        not stably diffeomorphic, where stabilising means taking connected sum with copies of S 2 × S 2 .
        We show that every closed, orientable 3-manifold admits such fillings, as do certain families of
        nonorientable 3-manifolds. In contrast we show that for a 3-manifold containing a 2-sided RP2 ,
        any two smooth, homeomorphic fillings are stably diffeomorphic.




                                             1. Introduction
  A filling of a closed, smooth 3-manifold Y is a smooth, compact 4-manifold M with ∂M = Y .
We prove the following.
Theorem 1.1. Let Y be a closed, smooth 3-manifold. Then Y admits a pair of fillings that are
homeomorphic rel. boundary but not stably diffeomorphic rel. boundary if one of the following holds.
  (i) Y is orientable.
 (ii) Y is a circle bundle over a closed surface F ̸= RP2 .
(iii) Y admits a null-bordant tangential Pin+ structure.
   Here two fillings M and M ′ of Y are stably diffeomorphic rel. boundary if there exists k ≥ 0 such
that M #k(S 2 × S 2 ) and M ′ #k(S 2 × S 2 ) are diffeomorphic via a diffeomorphism restricting to the
identity on the boundary. Stable homeomorphism, which is used later, is defined analogously. Note
that the fillings in Theorem 1.1 are in particular exotic fillings. By a theorem of Gompf [Gom84],
homeomorphism implies stable diffeomorphism for compact, orientable 4-manifolds, so the fillings
we produce in Theorem 1.1 are necessarily nonorientable.
   Every orientable 3-manifold admits a null-bordant tangential Pin+ structure, so Theorem 1.1 (i)
is implied by Theorem 1.1 (iii). We state (i) separately for emphasis, and because we give the
proof for this case separately, in Section 3.
   Our examples will be of the form
                                M = Z#K3 and M ′ = Z#11(S 2 × S 2 ),
for a suitable nonorientable filling Z of Y , where K3 denotes the Kummer surface. The first
examples of this sort, for closed 4-manifolds, are due to Kreck [Kre84]. Using that K3 splits
topologically as E8 #E8 #3(S 2 × S 2 ), we will show in Lemma 3.1 that M is homeomorphic to M ′ .
But by Rochlin’s theorem, there is no such smooth splitting of K3 . This is used in the proof of
Theorem 1.1, for Y satisfying (i), (ii), or (iii), and well-chosen fillings Z, to show that the union
                                                                                 Top
M ∪Y M ′ is nontrivial when considered in the kernel ker(Ω4 (ξG ) → Ω4 (ξG           )) of the forgetful
map between smooth and topological bordism groups over certain fibrations, defined in Section 2
and dependent on G = π1 (Z). Using a result of Kreck [Kre99, Corollary 3] (see Theorem 2.4 for
details), we show how unions in this kernel give rise to the eponymous stably exotic fillings of Y ,
namely fillings that are stably homeomorphic but not stably diffeomorphic, both rel. boundary.
Working stably is thus the most natural setting in which to isolate this type of exotic behaviour,
arising from Rochlin’s theorem, since it factors out the effect of gauge theory.
   The above strategy does not always produce stably exotic fillings, and indeed not all 3-manifolds
admit them.
Theorem 1.2. Let Y be a closed, smooth 3-manifold that contains a two-sided RP2 . Then Y does
not admit stably exotic fillings.

  Key words and phrases. 4-manifolds, exotic fillings.

    Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 partially answer the following question, which remains open in general.
Question 1.3. Which closed, smooth 3-manifolds admit stably exotic fillings?
   For example, we do not know whether the 3-manifold constructed in Example 6.8, a T 2 -bundle
over S 1 , admits stably exotic fillings.
   We also remark that it is open which 3-manifolds admit exotic fillings, i.e. fillings that are home-
omorphic rel. boundary but not diffeomorphic rel. boundary; cf. [EMM22; BKR26, Problem 4.6].
Another related open question asks which orientable 3-manifolds admit exotic orientable fillings.

Proof strategy. We now elaborate further on the proofs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.2. For the ar-
                                                                                                 Top
gument outlined on the previous page to work, at a minimum the kernel of Ω4 (ξG ) → Ω4 (ξG           )
must have a nontrivial element. Given any group G, together with a choice of abstract normal
1-type data (see Section 2), we can hope to characterise precisely when this kernel is nontrivial, by
considering differentials in the James spectral sequence computing Ω4 (ξG ), as in [KP25]. Nontriv-
iality of the kernel turns out to be equivalent to [K3 ] ̸= 0 in Ω4 (ξG ). Given a 3-manifold Y , we
can then seek to find, as we will do in the proof of Theorem 1.1, a suitable group G with normal
1-type data compatible with Y , and a suitable nonorientable filling Z with π1 (Z) = G, to realise
the nontrivial element of the kernel by the manifold M ∪Y M ′ described above. This will prove we
have constructed stably exotic fillings. In contrast, in the proof of Theorem 1.2, we show that in
the presence of RP2 × I ⊆ Y , for any possible ξG we will have [K3 ] = 0 ∈ Ω4 (ξG ). See Section 2 for
                                Top
more information on ξG and ξG       , and Section 4 for our compatibility condition for normal 1-type
data with Y .

The cardinality of stably exotic fillings. To supplement the results above, within a fixed
(stable) homeomorphism class of fillings, we show in Proposition 8.1 that there are at most two
stable diffeomorphism classes rel. boundary. So it is not possible to find any larger classes of stably
exotic fillings than we find in Theorem 1.1. On the other hand, in Proposition 8.3 we show that
modifying any given stably exotic pair by connected summing both with copies of S 1 × S 3 , one
can obtain infinitely many stable homeomorphism classes of pairs of stably exotic fillings for any
fixed Y that admits them, distinguished by their fundamental groups.

Examples. Now we give some examples designed to illustrate the use of condition (iii) in Theo-
rem 1.1 and to compare the three conditions of Theorem 1.1. As mentioned earlier, Theorem 1.1 (iii)
implies Theorem 1.1 (i). There is some overlap between (i) and (ii): for example, (i) implies (ii)
when F = S 2 . But in general both set differences between conditions (i) and (ii) are nonempty.
Since Theorem 1.1 (ii) does not imply Theorem 1.1 (i) while Theorem 1.1 (iii) does imply Theo-
rem 1.1 (i), one sees that Theorem 1.1 (ii) does not imply Theorem 1.1 (iii).
   Condition (iii) in Theorem 1.1 may seem difficult to check at first glance, in which case the
following observations, which we use in the proofs of the upcoming examples, may help. First,
Y admits a tangential Pin+ structure if and only if the orientation character w1Y : π1 (Y ) → Z/2
factors through Z/4 (Proposition 5.9). Second, a Pin+ 3-manifold is null-bordant if and only if the
spin surface dual to the orientation character is spin null-bordant (Proposition 5.10).
   In the following example, we describe a family of Pin+ nonorientable 3-manifolds admitting sta-
bly exotic fillings, by applying Theorem 1.1 (iii). This demonstrates that there exist nonorientable
3-manifolds admitting a null-bordant tangential Pin+ structure, so Theorem 1.1 (i) does not imply
Theorem 1.1 (iii).
Example 1.4. Let F be a closed, orientable surface and let F → Y → S 1 be a fibre bundle
with orientation-reversing monodromy φ : F → F . Note that Y is nonorientable by construction.
                                               ∗
Suppose that the fixed subgroup H 1 (F ; Z/2)φ is at least half-rank in H 1 (F ; Z/2). We show in
Proposition 6.6 that Y admits a null-bordant Pin+ structure, and hence admits stably exotic fillings
by Theorem 1.1 (iii). We show in Example 6.8 that the statement is false in general without the
                                 ∗
rank assumption on H 1 (F ; Z/2)φ .
   Next we give an example of a circle bundle over a surface (̸= RP2 ) which does not admit a
tangential Pin+ structure. This shows that Theorem 1.1 (iii) does not imply Theorem 1.1 (ii).
                              STABLY EXOTIC FILLINGS OF 3-MANIFOLDS                                    3


Example 1.5. Let F = #3 RP2 be the closed surface of nonorientable genus three and Y := S 1 ×F .
In Proposition 6.9 we show that the orientation character w1Y : π1 (Y ) → Z/2 does not factor
through Z/4. By Proposition 5.9, this shows that Y does not admit a tangential Pin+ structure.
   We have therefore shown that the only logical dependency between the items of Theorem 1.1 is
the aforementioned fact that Theorem 1.1 (iii) implies Theorem 1.1 (i).
Organisation. In Section 2 we introduce the key concept of normal 1-type data and explain the
significance of this concept to the paper. In Section 3 we prove the orientable case of Theorem 1.1.
In Section 4 we relate the existence of stably exotic fillings to the existence of stably exotic closed
4-manifolds, under certain hypotheses. The main result is the partial characterisation in Theo-
rem 4.5. In Section 5.1, we apply Theorem 4.5 to prove Theorem 1.1 (ii), the circle bundle case.
In Section 5.2, we prove Theorem 1.1 (iii). In Section 6 we provide the examples promised in
Examples 1.4 and 1.5. In Section 7, we prove Theorem 1.2. Finally in Section 8, we consider the
number of stably exotic fillings of a given 3-manifold.
Conventions. We assume that all 3-manifolds are closed, connected, and smooth, and that all
4-manifolds are compact, connected, and smooth.

that we use. MP was partially supported by EPSRC grant EP/T028335/2.

                                     2. Normal 1-type data
    Given a 3-manifold Y , our strategy to prove that it admits stably exotic fillings requires, of
course, the construction of stably homeomorphic fillings M and M ′ , together with some obstruc-
tion to stable diffeomorphism. The first component will be furnished by a lemma of Kreck, detailed
below as Lemma 3.1. For the second component, we exploit the fact that stably homeomorphic
fillings M and M ′ are stably diffeomorphic rel. Y if and only if M ∪Y M ′ is null-bordant over the nor-
mal 1-type of M (which is the same as the normal 1-type of M ′ as they are stably homeomorphic);
see Theorem 2.4. We will first recall some general facts about normal 1-types of manifolds [Kre99].
We then recall some specific ideas for working with normal 1-types of manifolds with spin universal
cover, developed by Teichner [Tei92].
2.1. Normal 1-types.
Definition 2.1. A normal 1-type for a smooth manifold W is a pair (B, ξ), where B is a space
with the homotopy type of a CW complex, ξ : B → BO is a 2-coconnected fibration with connected
fibre, and there exists a 2-connected map ν W : W → B, such that ξ ◦ ν W represents the stable
normal bundle νW : W → BO of W . Such a pair (W, ν W ) is called a normal 1-smoothing of W .
   A topological normal 1-type for a manifold W is a pair (B Top , ξ Top ), where B Top is a space
with the homotopy type of a CW complex, ξ Top : B Top → BTop is a 2-coconnected fibration with
connected fibre, and there exists a 2-connected map ν Top
                                                        W : W → B
                                                                       Top
                                                                           , such that ξ Top ◦ ν Top
                                                                                                 W
represents the stable normal microbundle νW : W → BTop of W . Such a pair (W, ν Top
                                           Top
                                                                                      W ) is called
a topological normal 1-smoothing of W .
   Here BTop is the classifying space for Top, the colimit under inclusion of the groups Top(n)
for n ≥ 0, consisting of homeomorphisms of Rn preserving 0.
Remark 2.2. It follows from the Moore–Postnikov factorisation (see e.g. [Bau77]) that every smooth
manifold W has a corresponding normal 1-type, and similarly every topological manifold W ad-
mits a topological normal 1-type. This theory also guarantees uniqueness, up to fibre homotopy
equivalence, of these objects.
Definition 2.3. Let W be a smooth manifold and let (B, ξ) be the normal 1-type of some smooth
manifold, not necessarily of W . A lift of the stable normal bundle of W to B is called a ξ-structure.
  The relevance of the normal 1-type technology to this article comes from the following theorem.
4               DANIEL KASPROWSKI, PATRICK ORSON, MARK POWELL, AND ARUNIMA RAY


Theorem 2.4 ([Kre99, Corollary 3; CS11, Lemma 2.2]).
 (i) Let M and M ′ be compact, smooth 4-manifolds with fixed identifications ∂M = Y = ∂M ′ ,
     and the same normal 1-type ξ : B → BO. Then M and M ′ are stably diffeomorphic rel. Y
     if and only if there exist normal 1-smoothings ν M and ν M ′ , of M and M ′ respectively, that
     agree on Y , such that
                                    [M ∪Y M ′ , ν M ∪ −ν M ′ ] = 0 ∈ Ω4 (ξ).
    (ii) Let M and M ′ be compact, topological 4-manifolds with fixed identifications ∂M = Y = ∂M ′ ,
         and the same topological normal 1-type ξ Top : B Top → BTop. Then M and M ′ are stably
         homeomorphic rel. Y if and only if there exist topological normal 1-smoothings ν Top     Top
                                                                                          M and ν M ′ ,
                    ′
         of M and M respectively, that agree on Y , such that
                                  [M ∪Y M ′ , ν Top    Top
                                                M ∪ −ν M ′ ] = 0 ∈ Ω4 (ξ
                                                                         Top
                                                                             ).
2.2. Normal 1-type data. When the universal cover of a manifold W is spin, there exists a 2-
connected classifying map c : W → Bπ1 (W ), and unique cohomology classes wiW ∈ H i (π1 (W ); Z/2),
for i = 1, 2, such that c∗ (wiW ) = wi (νW ), where νW denotes the stable normal bundle of W . In this
case, the fibre homotopy type of the normal 1-type is determined by the isomorphism class of the
triple (π1 (W ), w1W , w2W ), in both the smooth and topological categories [Tei92, Theorem 2.2.1 (a)].
   Using this, we can describe an algebraic abstraction that will permit us to consider putative
4-manifold fillings of 3-manifolds. The following definitions are due to Teichner [Tei92, Theo-
rem 2.2.1 (b)(IV)].
Definition 2.5. A triple (G, w, v) consisting of a finitely presented group G, an element w ∈
H 1 (G; Z/2), and an element v ∈ H 2 (G; Z/2) is called normal 1-type data.
   Given normal 1-type data, we define an associated pair (BG , ξG ), where BG is a space homotopy
equivalent to a CW complex and ξG : BG → BO is a fibration, as follows. Represent (w, v) via a
map (w, v) : K(G, 1) −
                     → K(Z/2, 1) × K(Z/2, 2). Let P2 (−) : BO → K(Z/2, 1) × K(Z/2, 2) denote
the map from BO to its Postnikov 2-type. We write BG for the homotopy fibre in
                           ζG                    P2 (−)+(w×v)
                      BG −−→ BO ×K(G, 1) −−−−−−−−−→ K(Z/2, 1) × K(Z/2, 2),                        (2.6)
with ζG further assumed to be a fibration. Here the operation + uses the H-space structure on
K(Z/2, 1) × K(Z/2, 2). Define the fibration
                                         ξG := pr1 ◦ ζG : BG → BO .

   We similarly define an associated pair (BG  , ξG ), where BG   is a space homotopy equivalent

   For a smooth manifold W whose universal cover is spin, the respective normal 1-type and

Theorem 2.2.1 (b)(IV)]. This explains the following definition.
Definition 2.9. Let W be a smooth manifold with universal cover spin. If the abstract normal
1-type data (G, w, v) is isomorphic to (π1 (W ), w1W , w2W ), we will say that W has normal 1-type
data (G, w, v).

Teichner [Tei93, Section II]. For ξG and ξG nonorientable, if there exists a vector bundle E →
K(G, 1) such that w1 (E) = w ∈ H 1 (G; Z/2) and w2 (E) = v ∈ H 2 (G; Z/2), then the adaptation
of the James spectral sequence was constructed in [Tei97, Before Lemma 2]. The general case was
constructed in detail by Galvin–Teichner–Veselá in [GTV26, Appendix B].
Remark 2.10. All 3-manifolds have universal cover spin because all orientable 3-manifolds are
spin. The fillings of 3-manifolds we will produce will have normal 1-types corresponding to the,
more algebraic, normal 1-type data we defined above. Hence we will not produce any fillings
with non-spin universal cover. It is possible that a 3-manifold might have a pair of exotic fillings
whose universal covers are non-spin. However such a pair would be stably diffeomorphic [Gom84;
FNOP25, Theorem 13.3], so the methods of this paper would not detect them. Hence from now
on we will only consider manifolds with spin universal cover.

               3. All orientable 3-manifolds admit stably exotic fillings
   We begin the proof of Theorem 1.1. We start with a lemma due to Kreck [Kre84], which gives
the key construction of potentially exotic nonorientable 4-manifolds, making use of the K3 surface.
This lemma will be used in this section and in subsequent sections.
Lemma 3.1 ([Kre84]). Let X be a compact, nonorientable 4-manifold. Let M := X#K3 and let
M ′ := X#11(S 2 × S 2 ). Then M and M ′ are homeomorphic (and hence stably homeomorphic) rel.
boundary.
Proof. We have
  M = X#K3 ∼  = X#E8 #E8 #3(S 2 × S 2 ) ∼
                                        = X#E8 #E 8 #3(S 2 × S 2 ) ∼
                                                                   = X#11(S 2 × S 2 ) = M ′ .
Here we use the classification of closed, simply connected 4-manifolds [Fre82], and the fact that
indefinite, symmetric, bilinear forms are determined up to isometry by their rank, signature, and
parity [MH73], to see that K3 ∼= E8 #E8 #3(S 2 ×S 2 ) and that E8 #E 8 #3(S 2 ×S 2 ) ∼
                                                                                     = #11(S 2 ×S 2 ).
To replace one copy of E8 by E 8 in the central homeomorphism we use that X is nonorientable, so
that the orientation of the 4-ball in X used for the connected sum can be reversed by an ambient
isotopy.                                                                                           □
  Using this lemma and Theorem 2.4, we can prove Theorem 1.1 (i).
Theorem 3.2. Let Y be a closed, orientable 3-manifold. Then Y admits a pair of stably exotic
fillings M and M ′ .
Proof. Since Y is orientable, it admits a compact, simply connected, spin filling X. Define
               M := X#(S 1 ×S
                           e 3 )#K3        and    M ′ := X#(S 1 ×S
                                                                e 3 )#11(S 2 × S 2 ),
where S 1 e×S 3 is the nonorientable S 3 bundle over S 1 . Then M and M ′ are homeomorphic by
Lemma 3.1, and they both have the normal 1-type data (Z, w, 0) with 0 ̸= w ∈ H 1 (Z; Z/2) ∼    = Z/2.
   If M and M ′ were stably diffeomorphic relative to Y , then by Theorem 2.4 (ii) there would exist
normal 1-smoothings ν M and ν M ′ of M and M ′ that agree on Y and such that [M ∪Y M ′ , ν M ∪
−ν M ′ ] = 0 ∈ Ω4 (ξZ ). We show next that this is not the case.
   Let ν M and ν M ′ be arbitrary normal 1-smoothings of M and M ′ that agree on Y . The

    4. A partial characterisation of 3-manifolds admitting stably exotic fillings
   In order to prove Theorem 1.1 (ii) and (iii), first we deduce a partial characterisation of 3-
manifolds admitting stably exotic fillings. As the universal cover of an arbitrary 3-manifold is
spin, the 3-manifold determines normal 1-type data as described in Section 2.2. Now we introduce
the notion of abstract normal 1-type data for a putative filling, whose normal 1-type data would
interact correctly with the normal 1-type of Y .
Definition 4.1. Let Y be a closed, smooth 3-manifold. The quadruple (G, w, v, φ) is called Y -
filling normal 1-type data if (G, w, v) comprises normal 1-type data (not necessarily for Y ), and
φ : π1 (Y ) → G is a homomorphism such that φ∗ (w) = w1Y ∈ H 1 (Y ; Z/2) and φ∗ (v) = w2Y ∈
H 2 (Y ; Z/2).
   In the definition above, one should think of G as the fundamental group of the putative filling
of Y , the map φ as the putative inclusion-induced map, and w and v as the putative first and
second Stiefel–Whitney classes of the filling.
Proposition 4.2. Let (G, w, v) and (H, x, y) be normal 1-type data. Let ϕ : G → H be a homo-
morphism such that ϕ∗ (x) = w and ϕ∗ (y) = v. Then there exists a map ϕB : BG → BH covering
IdBO ×ϕ : BO ×K(G, 1) → BO ×K(H, 1), up to homotopy. Since ξH is a fibration, we can assume
that ξH ◦ ϕB = ξG .
Proof. The assumption that ϕ∗ (x) = w and ϕ∗ (y) = v implies that the diagram
                                                 IdBO ×ϕ∗
                             BO ×K(G, 1)                      BO ×K(H, 1)
                                     P2 (−)+(w×v)                     P2 (−)+(x×y)
                                                    Id
                        K(Z/2, 1) × K(Z/2, 2)            K(Z/2, 1) × K(Z/2, 2)
commutes up to homotopy. Hence there is a map ϕB : BG → BH of the homotopy fibres covering
IdBO ×ϕ : BO ×K(G, 1) → BO ×K(H, 1) up to homotopy, as needed.                           □
Remark 4.3. When G is the trivial group, BG ≃ BSpin. Hence by choosing G to be the trivial group
in Proposition 4.2, we obtain a map BSpin → BH over BO, for any normal 1-type data (H, x, y).
This determines a map ΩSpin
                         4    → Ω4 (BH ), and so every spin 4-manifold has a ξH -structure. In the
proof of Theorem 3.2 we produced an instance of this map for H = Z by analysing the James
spectral sequence; this method generalises to arbitrary H.
Corollary 4.4. Let Y be a closed, smooth 3-manifold and let (H, x, y, φ) be Y -filling normal 1-type
data. Then there is a map φB : BY → BG over BO inducing φ on fundamental groups. Hence,
for every normal 1-smoothing ν Y of Y , we obtain a corresponding ξG -structure φB ◦ ν Y : Y → BG
inducing φ on fundamental groups.
                              STABLY EXOTIC FILLINGS OF 3-MANIFOLDS                                     7


Proof. Apply Proposition 4.2 with (G, w, v) the normal 1-type data of Y , with φ in place of ϕ. □
   Corollary 4.4 produces ξG -structures ν φ that might satisfy the hypotheses of (ii) in the following
promised partial characterisation of 3-manifolds admitting stably exotic fillings.
Theorem 4.5. Let Y be a closed, smooth 3-manifold and let (G, w, v, φ) be Y -filling normal 1-type
data.
  (i) If Y admits stably exotic fillings with normal 1-type data (G, w, v), then there exist closed
      stably exotic 4-manifolds with normal 1-type data (G, w, v).
 (ii) If φ is surjective and [Y, ν φ ] = 0 ∈ Ω3 (ξG ) for some ξG -structure ν φ : Y → BG inducing φ
      on fundamental groups, and there exist closed stably exotic 4-manifolds with normal 1-type
      data (G, w, v), then Y admits stably exotic fillings with normal 1-type data (G, w, v).
   We will use Theorem 4.5 to deduce the remaining items of Theorem 1.1 in Section 5.1, and to
prove Theorem 1.2 in Section 7.
Proof. First we prove (i). Assume that Y admits stably exotic fillings M and M ′ with normal
1-type data (G, w, v). Since M and M ′ are stably homeomorphic rel. Y , by Theorem 2.4 (i) there
exist normal 1-smoothings ν Top
                              M : M → BG
                                            Top
                                                and ν Top    ′     Top           Top      Top
                                                      M ′ : M → BG , such that ν M |Y = ν M ′ |Y ,
and such that
                             [M ∪Y M ′ , ν Top     Top             Top
                                           M ∪ −ν M ′ ] = 0 ∈ Ω4 (ξG ).
                                      Top
Recall that the spaces BG and BG          were constructed as certain homotopy fibres in Section 2.2,
differing only in that we used BO or BTop in the construction respectively. As such, the obstruc-
                                                                                               Top
tion to lifting topological normal 1-smoothings along the forgetful map ηG : BG → BG               is the
obstruction to lifting the stable topological normal bundle along the forgetful map BO → BTop,
which is, by definition, the Kirby–Siebenmann invariant of the manifold. Since both M and M ′
are smooth, this obstruction vanishes for each of ν Top           Top

and ν M ′ = ηG ◦ ν M .′

     Since M and M ′ are not stably diffeomorphic rel. Y , Theorem 2.4 (ii) implies that [M ∪Y

M , ν M ∪−ν M ′ ] ̸= 0 ∈ Ω4 (ξG ). Hence there exists a nontrivial element in the kernel of the forgetful
                                 Top
map Ω4 (ηG ) : Ω4 (ξG ) → Ω4 (ξG     ). Each element of Ω4 (ξG ) can be represented by a 4-manifold
with normal 1-type data (G, w, v), by surgery below the middle dimension. Apply this to surger
the trivial element M ∪Y M and the nontrivial element M ∪Y M ′ of Ω4 (ξG ) we just constructed to
obtain 4-manifolds with normal 1-type data (G, w, v). Automorphisms of the normal 1-type cannot
relate a nontrivial element of Ω4 (ξG ) with the trivial element. Hence by [Kre99, Theorem C], there
exist closed stably exotic 4-manifolds with normal 1-type data (G, w, v). This completes the proof
of (i).
     Next we prove (ii). If w = 0, then closed stably exotic 4-manifolds with normal 1-type data
(G, w, v) do not exist by [Gom84]. Hence we assume w ̸= 0. By our hypothesis that [Y, ν φ ] = 0 ∈
Ω3 (ξG ) for some ξG -structure ν φ of Y , there exists a filling X of Y with a smoothing ν X : X → BG
lifting the stable normal bundle along ξG and extending ν φ on Y . Using surgery, we can assume
that ν X is a normal 1-smoothing, i.e. is 2-connected (recall from Remark 2.8 that π2 (BG ) = 0). It
follows from the definition of ξG and the assumption that w ̸= 0 that w1 (νX) ̸= 0, and hence X
is nonorientable. Define
                              M := X#K3 and M ′ := X#11(S 2 × S 2 ).
Then M and M ′ are homeomorphic by Lemma 3.1.
  Extend ν X to normal 1-smoothings ν M and ν M ′ of M and M ′ respectively. For this, use the
unique spin structures on K3 and 11(S 2 × S 2 ) together with Remark 4.3 to obtain ξG -structures
on these manifolds, and take the connected sum. Again both normal 1-smoothings agree with ν φ
on Y . For those smoothings,
                              [M ∪Y M ′ , ν M ∪ −ν M ′ ] = [K3 ] ∈ Ω4 (ξG ),
because the double [X ∪Y X, ν X ∪ −ν X ] is null-bordant, as is #11(S 2 × S 2 ).
   Now we show that M and M ′ , which both have normal 1-type data (G, w, v), are the desired
stably exotic fillings. Suppose then, for a contradiction, that there exists a stable diffeomorphism
8              DANIEL KASPROWSKI, PATRICK ORSON, MARK POWELL, AND ARUNIMA RAY


from M to M ′ relative to Y , i.e. a diffeomorphism f : M #ℓ(S 2 × S 2 ) → M ′ #ℓ(S 2 × S 2 ) for some
ℓ ∈ N0 . We use this to prove that there are no closed, stably exotic 4-manifolds with normal 1-type
data (G, w, v), which contradicts the hypotheses of (ii), and thus completes the proof.
   By [KP25, Proposition 4.1 (ii)], if [K3 ] = 0 ∈ Ω4 (ξG ), then there are no closed, stably exotic
4-manifolds with normal 1-type data (G, w, v). So we aim to prove the former statement.
   We claim that ν M ′ #ℓ(S 2 ×S 2 ) ◦ f and ν M #ℓ(S 2 ×S 2 ) are homotopic rel. Y . For this we use that
both restrict to ν φ on the boundary and that φ : π1 (Y ) → G is surjective by assumption, which
implies that the inclusion Y → M #ℓ(S 2 × S 2 ) is 1-connected. Consider the diagram
                                                           νφ
                                         Y                                     BG
                                                                                 ξG

                                 M #ℓ(S 2 × S 2 )         νM #ℓ(S 2 ×S 2 )     BO .

The maps ν M #ℓ(S 2 ×S 2 ) and ν M ′ #ℓ(S 2 ×S 2 ) ◦ f both give examples of the diagonal dashed arrow
that make the diagram commute. Let F be the homotopy fibre of ξG . The obstructions to finding
a homotopy rel. Y between two given lifts of νM #ℓ(S 2 ×S 2 ) along ξG lie in

                                        H i (M #ℓ(S 2 × S 2 ), Y ; πi (F )).

Since ξG is 2-coconnected we have that πi (F ) = 0 for i ≥ 2. Since Y → M #ℓ(S 2 × S 2 ) is 1-
connected, the cohomology groups H 1 (M #ℓ(S 2 ×S 2 ), Y ; π1 (F )) and H 0 (M #ℓ(S 2 ×S 2 ), Y ; π0 (F ))
both vanish. Hence any two lifts, in particular ν M #ℓ(S 2 ×S 2 ) and ν M ′ #ℓ(S 2 ×S 2 ) ◦ f , are homotopic
rel. Y .
   It follows that

     0 = [M #ℓ(S 2 × S 2 ) ∪Y M ′ #ℓ(S 2 × S 2 ), ν M #ℓ(S 2 ×S 2 ) ∪ −ν M ′ #ℓ(S 2 ×S 2 ) ] = [K3 ] ∈ Ω4 (ξG ),

as desired. Hence, by [KP25, Proposition 4.1], there exist no closed stably exotic 4-manifolds with
normal 1-type data (G, w, v).                                                                    □


         5. Some nonorientable 3-manifolds that admit stably exotic fillings
   In this section we prove Theorem 1.1 (ii) and (iii), using Theorem 4.5 (ii). Recall that the latter
result has two main hypotheses. One of these is the existence of closed stably exotic 4-manifolds.
To arrange for this, we will leverage the following statements from [Kre84] and [KP25]. Recall that
H i (Z/2; Z/2) = Z/2 for i = 1, 2.

Theorem 5.1 ([Kre84]). There exist closed stably exotic 4-manifolds with normal 1-type data
(Z/2, 1, 1).

    For example, RP4 #K3 and RP4 #11(S 2 × S 2 ) are stably exotic.

Theorem 5.2 ([KP25, Theorem A]). Let (G, w, v) be normal 1-type data. If there exist closed
stably exotic 4-manifolds with normal 1-type data (G, w, v), then w ̸= 0 and w3 = wv ∈ H 3 (G; Z/2).
   If moreover G has cohomological dimension at most 3, the converse also holds, i.e. if w ̸= 0
and w3 = wv ∈ H 3 (G; Z/2) then there exist closed stably exotic 4-manifolds with normal 1-type
data (G, w, v).

   In Section 5.1 we prove Theorem 1.1 (ii). We use Theorem 5.2 to show the existence of closed
stably exotic 4-manifolds. The key observation is that circle bundles over aspherical surfaces
provide surjective maps φ : π1 (Y ) → G, for groups G with cohomological dimension two, that are
compatible with the normal 1-type data in the sense of Definition 4.1.
   In Section 5.2, we prove Theorem 1.1 (iii) for nonorientable Y , the case of orientable Y having
been already dealt with in Section 3. In this case, we apply Theorem 5.1 to provide the closed
stably exotic 4-manifolds required for Theorem 4.5 (ii). To satisfy the other hypothesis of the
latter theorem, we use the normal 1-type data (Z/2, 1, 1), and connect Ω3 (ξZ/2 ) to Pin+-bordism.
                             STABLY EXOTIC FILLINGS OF 3-MANIFOLDS                                    9


5.1. Circle bundles admit stably exotic fillings. The next result proves Theorem 1.1 (ii).
Theorem 5.3. Let Y be a circle bundle over a surface Σ ̸= RP2 . Then Y admits stably exotic
fillings.
Proof. If Σ ∼
            = S 2 then Y is orientable, and this case was covered in Theorem 3.2. Hence we assume
for this proof that Σ is aspherical.
   Let p : X → Σ be the total space of the disc bundle over Σ obtained from Y by filling in each fibre
with D2 . This is possible since Diff(S 1 ) ≃ O(2). Then the universal cover X  e ≃Σ e is contractible,
                                                      ∼
and in particular is spin. Furthermore, π1 (X) = π1 (Σ), and hence π1 (X) is cohomologically 2-
dimensional. Let i : Y → X be the inclusion map and consider the Y -filling normal 1-type data
given by (G, w, v, φ) := (π1 (X), w1X , w2X , π1 (i)). Note that w3 = wv ∈ H 3 (G; Z/2) automatically
since H 3 (G; Z/2) = 0. Hence by Theorem 5.2 there exist closed stably exotic 4-manifolds with
normal 1-type data (G, w, v). This gives one of the hypotheses needed to apply Theorem 4.5 (ii).
   The map φ : π1 (Y ) → G = π1 (X) is surjective by construction. The 4-manifold X shows that Y
bounds over the normal 1-type. Thus all the hypotheses Theorem 4.5 (ii) are satisfied, and so Y
admits stably exotic fillings.                                                                       □
5.2. Pin bordism and stably exotic fillings. We will soon prove Theorem 1.1 (iii). To do
so, we will require the following facts about Pin structures and Pin bordism groups from Kirby–
Taylor [KT90]. Let Y be a manifold with stable tangent bundle T Y and stable normal bundle νY .
Proposition 5.4 ([KT90, Lemma 1.7]). Let Y be a manifold. Let ζ denote a (stable) vector bundle
over Y with determinant bundle det(ζ).
  (i) A Pin+ structure on ζ is equivalent to a spin structure on ζ ⊕ 3 det(ζ). Such a structure exists
      if and only if w2 (ζ) = 0.
 (ii) A Pin− structure on ζ is equivalent to a spin structure on ζ ⊕ det(ζ). Such a structure exists
      if and only if w2 (ζ) + w1 (ζ)2 = 0.
  Here is an immediate corollary.
Corollary 5.5. Let Y be a manifold with stable tangent bundle T Y and stable normal bundle νY .
  (i) The manifold Y admits a tangential Pin+ structure if and only if w2 (T Y ) = 0, if and only if
      w2 (νY ) + w1 (νY )2 = 0, if and only if Y admits an normal Pin− structure.
 (ii) The manifold Y admits a tangential Pin− structure if and only if w2 (T Y ) + w1 (T Y )2 = 0, if
      and only if w2 (νY ) = 0, if and only if Y admits an normal Pin+ structure.
Remark 5.6. The usual convention is to write wi (Y ) := wi (T Y ), but since the normal bundle also
plays a large rôle in this article we preserve the T in the notation to avoid potential confusion.
Proposition 5.7 ([KT90, §2]). Every 3-manifold Y has a tangential Pin− structure, and it has a
tangential Pin+ structure if and only if w12 (T Y ) = 0.
Proof. Details were not given in [KT90], so we provide them here. In this proof, for brevity, denote
vi := vi (T Y ) and wi := wi (T Y ) for the Wu and Stiefel–Whitney classes respectively. We similarly
omit T Y from the notation for the total Wu and Stiefel–Whitney classes.
    First, we show that v2 = 0. By definition of the Wu class, we have that v2 ∪ x = Sq2 (x) for
every x ∈ H 1 (Y ; Z/2), and Sq2 (x) = 0 because Sq2 always vanishes on H 1 . By Poincaré duality it
follows that v2 = 0 as claimed.
    The Wu formula for the total classes is w = Sq(v). From this we can compute that v1 = w1 and
w2 = v2 + Sq1 (v1 ) = v2 + w12 , hence v2 = w2 + w12 , as we are working over Z/2. Now since v2 = 0
we must have w2 + w12 = 0, so every 3-manifold admits a tangential Pin− structure. Also w2 = 0
if and only if w12 = 0, so a 3-manifold admits a tangential Pin+ structure if and only if w12 = 0. □
Lemma 5.8. Let Y be a manifold. We have that w12 (T Y ) = 0 if and only if w1 (T Y ) : π1 (Y ) → Z/2
admits a lift to Z/4 along the surjective map Z/4 ↠ Z/2.
Proof. The exact sequence 0 → Z/2 → Z/4 → Z/2 → 0 yields an exact sequence
                                                          β
                            H 1 (Y ; Z/4) → H 1 (Y ; Z/2) −
                                                          → H 2 (Y ; Z/2),
10             DANIEL KASPROWSKI, PATRICK ORSON, MARK POWELL, AND ARUNIMA RAY


where β denotes the Bockstein homomorphism. It is a standard property of Steenrod squares (see
e.g. [Hat02, Section 4L]) that β = Sq1 . By the universal coefficient theorem and since Z/4 and
Z/2 are abelian, we thus have the exact sequence
                                                                     β=Sq1
                    Hom(π1 (Y ), Z/4)            Hom(π1 (Y ), Z/2)           H 2 (Y ; Z/2).

We see from the sequence that w1 (T Y ) ∈ Hom(π1 (Y ), Z/2) lifts to a map to Z/4 if and only if
w12 (T Y ) = Sq1 (w1 (T Y )) = β(w1 (T Y )) = 0.                                              □
     We deduce the following characterisation for when tangential Pin+ structures exist on 3-manifolds.
Proposition 5.9. A closed, nonorientable 3-manifold Y admits a tangential Pin+ structure if and
only if the orientation character w : π1 (Y ) ↠ Z/2 factors as π1 (Y ) → Z/4 ↠ Z/2.
Proof. Combine Proposition 5.7 and Lemma 5.8.                                                            □
   This will be used in Section 6, when we seek to apply Theorem 5.12 below. The following is
also from Kirby–Taylor [KT90].
Proposition 5.10 ([KT90, Theorems 5.1 and 5.2]).
                                    + ∼
  (i) There are isomorphisms ΩPin
                                      =
                                      → ΩSpin
                                      −         ∼

Remark 5.11. It is also true that ΩPin
                                   4    = 0. For the purposes of this paper, this explains why it is
not so helpful to look at Pin− structures, even though every 3-manifold admits a Pin− structure.
     The following theorem proves Theorem 1.1 (iii).
Theorem 5.12. Let Y be a closed 3-manifold. If Y admits a null-bordant tangential Pin+ structure,
then Y admits stably exotic fillings.
Proof. We already proved Theorem 5.12 in the case that Y is orientable, in Theorem 3.2. Hence
we can restrict here to the case that Y is nonorientable.
   Let φ : π1 (Y ) ↠ Z/2 be the orientation character of Y . Here φ is surjective since Y is nonori-
entable. Let ξZ/2 be the normal 1-type for the normal 1-type data (Z/2, w = 1, v = 1), constructed
as described in Section 2.2. Here w ∈ H 1 (Z/2; Z/2) ∼     = Z/2 and v ∈ H 2 (Z/2; Z/2) ∼    = Z/2 are the
generators.
   We claim that [Y, ν φ ] = 0 ∈ Ω3 (ξZ/2 ) for some ξZ/2 -structure ν φ inducing φ : π1 (Y ) → π1 (BZ/2 ) =
Z/2. Indeed, let X be a (hypothesised) tangential Pin+ filling of Y , and let w1X : X → K(Z/2, 1)
be the map corresponding to the orientation character of X, which is such that the composition
                                                         1(wX )∗
                                      π1 (Y ) → π1 (X) −−− −→ Z/2                                   (5.13)
                                             +                                          2
equals φ. Since X has a tangential Pin structure, X    e is spin and w1 (νX) + w2 (νX) = 0 by
Corollary 5.5 (i). Using the cup product structure on K(Z/2, 1) ≃ RP∞ , naturality, the fact that
w pulls back to w1 (νX), and finally the previous sentence, we therefore have
             (w1X )∗ (v) = (w1X )∗ (w2 ) = (w1X )∗ (w)2 = w1 (νX)2 = w2 (νX) ∈ H 2 (X; Z/2).
By Proposition 4.2 we obtain a map (w1X )B : Bπ1 (X) → BZ/2 over BO that induces (w1X )∗ on
fundamental groups. Thus X admits a ξZ/2 -structure (w1X )B ◦ ν X , where ν X is a normal 1-
smoothing of X. This ξZ/2 -structure on X induces a ξZ/2 -structure ν φ on Y that gives φ on
fundamental groups by (5.13). We see that X is a null-bordism witnessing that [Y, ν φ ] = 0 ∈
Ω3 (ξZ/2 ). This completes the proof of the claim.
   We know from Theorem 5.1 that the normal 1-type data (Z/2, 1, 1) admits closed stably exotic
4-manifolds. Hence we may apply Theorem 4.5 (ii) to see that Y admits stably exotic fillings. □
Remark 5.14. There is a free transitive action of H 1 (Y ; Z/2) on the set of Pin+ structures, and in
applications of Theorem 5.12, once we know that Y admits a Pin+ structure, we are free to try to
modify it by this action to arrange for Y to be Pin+-null-bordant.

                                              6. Examples
   We provide the Pin+ examples promised in the introduction. The first aim is to prove that
the examples in Example 1.4 behave as asserted. For this we need a couple of lemmas, before
Proposition 6.6, which is the main result of this section.
   First, we set up some notation. Let F be a closed, orientable surface of genus g. For a Z/2
vector space P , we write P ∗ := HomZ/2 (P, Z/2) for the dual vector space. For any i ≥ 0, let
                    ∼
                    =
ev : H i (F ; Z/2) −→ Hi (F ; Z/2)∗ denote the evaluation map. We will consider the Z/2-valued
intersection form
                 λF : H1 (F ; Z/2) × H1 (F ; Z/2) → Z/2; (x, y) 7→ ev ◦P D−1 (y) (x)
                  Z/2                                                           

and the Poincaré dual cup product form
                 − ⌣ − : H 1 (F ; Z/2) × H 1 (F ; Z/2) → Z/2;   (f, h) 7→ ev(f ⌣ h)[F ]Z/2 .
Both can be represented by the diagonal sum of g copies of the standard symplectic matrix ( 01 10 ).
A Lagrangian for either pairing is a direct summand L with L = L⊥ . The proof we give of the
next lemma was suggested to us in this formulation by Csaba Nagy; it is closely related to the
proof of [Nag24, Theorem 7.6].
Lemma 6.1. Let (P, ψ) be a hyperbolic form over Z/2 of dimension 2g and let V be a subspace
of P of dimension at least g. Then there is a Lagrangian K ⊆ P such that K + V = P .
Proof. By passing to a g-dimensional subspace of V , without loss of generality we can assume that
V is rank g. Writing j : V → P for the inclusion, we have that V ⊥ is the kernel of the surjective
map j ∗ ◦ ad(ψ) : P → V ∗ , so dim V ⊥ = dim P − dim V ∗ = g = dim V . Let Z := V ∩ V ⊥ and choose
direct sum decompositions V = U ⊕ Z and V ⊥ = U ′ ⊕ Z, so that V + V ⊥ = Z ⊕ U ⊕ U ′ . Noting
that Z is the radical for the restriction of ψ to both V and to V ⊥ , we have that ψ restricts to a
nonsingular form on both U and U ′ . As U and U ′ have the same dimension, we may thus choose
an isomorphism of nonsingular alternating forms f : (U, ψ|U ) → (U ψ|U ′ ). Such an isomorphism
determines a Lagrangian ∆f := {(y, f (y)) | y ∈ U } ⊆ U ⊕ U ′ . By the same argument as the second
sentence of the proof, dim(U ⊕ U ′ )⊥ = dim P − dim(U ⊕ U ′ ). The restriction of ψ to U ⊕ U ′ is
nonsingular, so (U ⊕ U ′ ) ∩ (U ⊕ U ′ )⊥ = {0}. Combining the two previous sentences, we have
                                       P = (U ⊕ U ′ ) ⊕ (U ⊕ U ′ )⊥ .                          (6.2)
                                                                                     ′ ⊥
We will now extend ∆f to a full Lagrangian of (P, ψ). Note that Z ⊆ (U ⊕ U ) . Since dim U +
dim Z = dim V = g = dim V ⊥ = dim U ′ + dim Z we have that 2 dim Z = 2g − dim U − dim U ′ .
Also 2g = dim P = dim U + dim U ′ + dim(U ⊕ U ′ )⊥ , and hence dim(U ⊕ U ′ )⊥ = 2 dim Z, i.e.
Z ⊆ (U ⊕ U ′ )⊥ is half-rank. Moreover we already noted that ψ vanishes identically on Z, so
Z is isotropic. Since the decomposition in (6.2) is by definition orthogonal with respect to ψ,
and ψ is nonsingular, ψ restricts to a nonsingular form on (U ⊕ U ′ )⊥ . It follows that Z is a
Lagrangian for the restriction in (U ⊕ U ′ )⊥ . Moreover Z admits a complementary Lagrangian L,
so that Z ⊕ L = (U ⊕ U ′ )⊥ . To find one, start with a complementary summand L′ . Since ψ| is
nonsingular, Z → (L′ )∗ is an isomorphism, and hence by adding elements of Z to the elements of
a basis for L′ , we can change L′ to a Lagrangian L that is still complementary to Z.
   For any complementary Lagrangian L to Z in (U ⊕ U ′ )⊥ , the submodule
                                 K := ∆f ⊕ L ⊆ (U ⊕ U ′ ) ⊕ (U ⊕ U ′ )⊥
is a Lagrangian, and is such that K + V = P .                                                     □
   For a closed, orientable surface F , let
                 ad(− ⌣ −) : H 1 (F ; Z/2) → H 1 (F ; Z/2)∗ ; f 7→ (h 7→ ev(f ⌣ h)[F ]Z/2 )
denote the adjoint of the cup product form. Equivalently, f 7→ h ⌢ (f ⌢ [F ]Z/2 ).
Lemma 6.3. Let F be a closed, orientable surface of genus g. Let V be a summand of H 1 (F ; Z/2) ∼
                                                                                                 =
(Z/2)2g whose rank is at least g. Then there is a Lagrangian K ⊆ H 1 (F ; Z/2) of the cup product
form such that
                                                ad(−⌣−)
                             V ,→ H 1 (F ; Z/2) −−−−−−→ H 1 (F ; Z/2)∗ → K ∗
is surjective.
12               DANIEL KASPROWSKI, PATRICK ORSON, MARK POWELL, AND ARUNIMA RAY


Proof. By Lemma 6.1, there exists a Lagrangian K for the cup product form such that K + V =
H 1 (F ; Z/2). Since K is a Lagrangian, K ⊆ K ⊥ and hence the composition
                                                     ad(−⌣−)
                                 K ,→ H 1 (F ; Z/2) −−−−−−→ H 1 (F ; Z/2)∗ → K ∗                 (6.4)
is the zero map. We develop the diagram
                                      K +V                                          (K + V )/K
                                          ∼
                                          =
                                                     ∼
                                                     =
                     V             H 1 (F ; Z/2)              H 1 (F ; Z/2)∗           K ∗.
The bottom row is the composition in the statement of the lemma. The down-right-right compo-
sition K + V → K ∗ factors through (K + V )/K by (6.4), which defines the right vertical map.
We have labelled several maps as being surjective or isomorphisms. We see that the composition
K + V → K ∗ is surjective. It follows that the right vertical map (K + V )/K → K ∗ is surjective.
Moreover, observe that the upper composition V → K + V → (K + V )/K is surjective. It follows
that the lower composition V → K ∗ is surjective, as desired.                                  □
Corollary 6.5. Let F be a closed, orientable surface of genus g. Let V be a summand of
H 1 (F ; Z/2) ∼
              = (Z/2)2g of rank at least g. Then there is a Lagrangian L ⊆ H1 (F ; Z/2) of the

is surjective.
Proof. Let K ⊆ H 1 (F ; Z/2) be the Lagrangian as in Lemma 6.3, and define L := P D(K) ⊆
H1 (F ; Z/2). Since Poincaré duality determines an isometry from − ⌣ − to λZ/2 , L is a Lagrangian
of λZ/2 . We have the following diagram. It is straightforward to check that it commutes.

       f 7→ h 7→ h(f ⌢ [F ]Z/2 ) = h 7→ h ⌢ (f ⌢ [F ]Z/2 ) = h 7→ ev(h ⌣ f )[F ]Z/2 ,
and so is ad(− ⌣ −). Thus V surjects onto K ∗ in this diagram by Lemma 6.3, and hence by

     We are now ready to provide the examples promised in Example 1.4.
Proposition 6.6. Let F be a closed, orientable surface of genus g and let F → Y → S 1 be a
fibre bundle with orientation-reversing monodromy φ : F → F . Suppose that the fixed subgroup
              ∗
H 1 (F ; Z/2)φ ⊆ H 1 (F ; Z/2) has rank at least g. Then Y admits a null-bordant Pin+ structure,
and hence admits stably exotic fillings by Theorem 1.1 (iii).
Proof. The orientation character factors through the bundle projection map as
                                  π1 (Y ) → π1 (S 1 ) ∼
                                                      = Z ↠ Z/2.
Hence there is a lift to Z/4 and so there is a tangential Pin+ structure on Y by Proposition 5.9. A
copy of the fibre F is dual to w1 . This has an induced spin structure and, by Proposition 5.10 (i),
Y is Pin+ null-bordant if and only if F is spin null-bordant. To arrange the latter, we are free to
change the Pin+ structure on Y , and hence the induced spin structure on F , using the action of
H 1 (Y ; Z/2).
   We have a Wang exact sequence
                             0                                                       φ∗ −Id
            H 0 (F ; Z/2) −
                          → H 0 (F ; Z/2) → H 1 (Y ; Z/2) → H 1 (F ; Z/2) −−−−→ H 1 (F ; Z/2)    (6.7)
leading to a short exact sequence
                                                                                ∗
                                 0 → Z/2 → H 1 (Y ; Z/2) → H 1 (F ; Z/2)φ → 0,
                              STABLY EXOTIC FILLINGS OF 3-MANIFOLDS                                     13

                    ∗
where H 1 (F ; Z/2)φ denotes the fixed points under φ∗ .
                                                                                            ∗
   Let ι : F → Y be the inclusion. If Im ι∗ : H 1 (Y ; Z/2) → H 1 (F ; Z/2) = H 1 (F ; Z/2)φ ⊆
                                                                            

H 1 (F ; Z/2) is at least half-rank, then by Corollary 6.5, there is a Lagrangian L for the Z/2-
intersection form such that
                                      ∗                   ev
                        H 1 (F ; Z/2)φ → H 1 (F ; Z/2) −→ H1 (F ; Z/2)∗ → L∗
is surjective. The group H 1 (Y ; Z/2) acts transitively on the Pin+ structures on Y . The effect of
the action of x ∈ H 1 (Y ; Z/2) on a spin structure of F is the effect of ι∗ (x). We can therefore
make any change of spin structures on F that corresponds to the action of an element of Im ι∗ =
              ∗
H 1 (F ; Z/2)φ . Under the action, ι∗ (x) changes the spin structure on a curve γ ⊆ F if and only if
                                             ∗
ev ◦ι∗ (x)[γ] = 1 ∈ Z/2. Since H 1 (F ; Z/2)φ maps surjectively to L∗ , it follows that by changes of
the Pin+ structure on Y , we can change the spin structure induced on F to realise any desired spin
structure on the Lagrangian L. Specifically, we make the spin structure into the bounding one on
L. After that, F spin bounds, and hence Y admits a Pin+ filling by Proposition 5.10 (i).           □

   Next we give an example, also promised in Example 1.4, demonstrating that Proposition 6.6 is
                                                           ∗
false in general without the hypothesis that H 1 (F ; Z/2)φ is at least half-rank.
Example 6.8. Let F = T 2 be a torus. Let φ : F → F be a diffeomorphism whose induced
map on H 1 (F ; Z/2) is represented by ( 11 10 ), and consider the associated T 2 -bundle Y over S 1 . The
monodromy φ is orientation-reversing, and so Y is nonorientable. As in the proof of Proposition 6.6,
the orientation character factors through the bundle projection map as wY : π1 (Y ) → π1 (S 1 ) ∼       =
Z ↠ Z/2, so there is a lift to Z/4 and hence Y admits a tangential Pin+ structure by Proposition 5.9.
    One computes that φ∗ acts transitively on the nonzero elements of H 1 (F ; Z/2), and hence has
no nonzero fixed points; in particular the rank of the fixed points is 0 < g/2 = 1/2. By the Wang
sequence (6.7), the map H 1 (Y ; Z/2) → H 1 (F ; Z/2) is trivial, and hence every Pin+ structure on Y
induces the same spin structure on F . We need to determine the Arf invariant of this spin structure
to identify its spin bordism class. Since the action of φ∗ on H 1 (F ; Z/2) \ {0} is transitive, the only
spin structure that is invariant under φ∗ is the non-bounding structure on curves corresponding to
all three nontrivial elements (1, 0), (0, 1), and (1, 1) in (Z/2)2 ∼
                                                                   = H 1 (F ; Z/2). To see this, note that
all spin structures restrict to a non-bounding one on at least one of these three curves. This spin
structure has Arf invariant nonzero, and hence as a spin surface F is nontrivial in ΩSpin 2   . So Y does
not Pin+-bound, by Proposition 5.10 (i). Thus the assumption on the fixed points was necessary
in Proposition 6.6. We do not know whether this Y admits stably exotic fillings, for some other
normal 1-type data.
  Finally we construct a circle bundle over a surface (̸= RP2 ) which does not admit a tangential
Pin+ structure, as mentioned in Example 1.5.
Proposition 6.9. Let F = #3 RP2 be the closed surface of nonorientable genus three and let
Y := S 1 × F . The orientation character w1Y : π1 (Y ) → Z/2 does not factor through Z/4, and hence
Y does not admit a tangential Pin+ by Proposition 5.9.
Proof. The orientation character of F factors as
                                                               ∼
                                                               =        wY
                          w1F : π1 (F ) → π1 (F ) × π1 (S 1 ) −
                                                              → π1 (Y ) −−1→ Z/2.
Thus if w1Y factors through Z/4 then so does w1F . Write π1 (F ) = π1 (#3 RP2 ) ∼
                                                                                = ⟨a, b, c | a2 b2 c2 ⟩,
where the orientation character sends each of a, b, and c to 1. The orientation character of F
factors further through the Hurewicz map as
                                                                   wF
                                   w1F : π1 (F ) → H1 (F ; Z) −−→
                                                                1
                                                                  Z/2.
If w1F factors through Z/4, so does wF  1 ; since Z/4 is abelian, maps to it factor through the
                                                                  φ
abelianisation. Suppose there is such a factorisation H1 (F ; Z) −→ Z/4 → Z/2. The element
[abc] ∈ H1 (F ; Z) has order two, so we must have φ([abc]) = 2 ∈ Z/4, which maps trivially to
Z/2. This contradicts the fact that wF
                                     1 ([abc]) = 1 ∈ Z/2, which holds since each of a, b, and c are
orientation-reversing. Thus wF1 does not factor through Z/4, and hence neither does w1F .        □

     7. No stably exotic fillings in the presence of a two-sided projective plane
     We prove Theorem 1.2, whose statement we recall.
Theorem 1.2. Let Y be a closed 3-manifold that contains a two-sided RP2 . Then Y does not
admit stably exotic fillings.
Proof. Let X be a smooth filling of Y , which exists since the smooth bordism group of unoriented 3-
manifolds is trivial. If the universal cover X e is non-spin, then by [Gom84; FNOP25, Theorem 13.3],
any 4-manifold stably homeomorphic to X is stably diffeomorphic to X, and we are done. So we
may assume that X    e is spin.

   Let (G, w, v) be the normal 1-type data of X. Then by hypothesis we have maps RP2 −         →Y −  → X,

                        8. The cardinality of stably exotic fillings
   We consider the size of the set of stably exotic fillings of a given 3-manifold. First we show
there are at most two fillings up to stable diffeomorphism, within a fixed stable homeomorphism
class. Then we show that if Y admits stably exotic fillings, then it admits infinitely many stable
homeomorphism classes of such.
Proposition 8.1. Let Y be a closed 3-manifold and let M be a filling of Y . Let FY (M ) denote
the set of smooth fillings of Y that are stably homeomorphic to M rel. boundary, modulo stable
diffeomorphism rel. boundary. Then |FY (M )| ≤ 2.
Proof. After possibly stabilising, we can suppose that Y and M are such that there exists M ′
that is homeomorphic to M rel. boundary but not stably diffeomorphic rel. boundary; if not then
|FY (M )| = 1 and we are done. Let ξG : BG → BO be the normal 1-type of M , constructed using
                                      STABLY EXOTIC FILLINGS OF 3-MANIFOLDS                              15


the normal 1-type data (G := π1 (M ), w1M , w2M ), and let ν M be a normal 1-smoothing. Similarly,
      Top     Top
let ξG    : BG     → BTop be the topological normal 1-type of M , constructed in the same way.
                                                                     Top
   By Theorem 2.4, the forgetful map Ω4 (ηG ) : Ω4 (ξG ) → Ω4 (ξG        ) is not injective and hence
the kernel is isomorphic to Z/2, generated by K3 (with some normal 1-smoothing) by [KP25,
Proposition 4.1].
   Now let N be a smooth filling of Y that is stably homeomorphic to M rel. boundary. We will
show that N is stably diffeomorphic to either M or M ′ rel. boundary, which will complete the proof.
By Theorem 2.4 (ii), there exists a topological normal 1-smoothing ν Top  N   of N that is bordant to

If [M ∪Y N, ν M ∪ −ν N ] = 0 ∈ Ω4 (ξG ) then N is stably diffeomorphic to M rel. boundary by
Theorem 2.4 (i). If not, [M ∪Y N, ν M ∪ −ν N ] is nonzero in ker Ω4 (ηG ) ∼    = Z/2. Since M ′ is not
stably diffeomorphic to M rel. boundary, Theorem 2.4 (i) implies that [M ′ ∪Y M, ν M ′ ∪ −ν M ] is
nontrivial in Ω4 (ξG ) for any normal 1-smoothing ν M ′ that agrees with ν M on Y . Since M and
M ′ are homeomorphic, by the argument of the previous paragraph, with M ′ in place of N , there
exists such a normal 1-smoothing ν M ′ such that [M ′ ∪Y M, ν M ′ ∪ −ν M ] ∈ ker Ω4 (ηG ).
    Thus we have two representatives of the nontrivial element of ker Ω4 (ηG ) ∼  = Z/2, and so the sum
                           [M ′ ∪Y M, ν M ′ ∪ −ν M ] + [M ∪Y N, ν M ∪ −ν N ] ∈ Ω4 (ξG )              (8.2)
                                              ′
is trivial. Take the product of (M ∪Y M ) ⊔ (M ∪Y N ) with I, and glue (M × I, ν M ◦ pr1 ) to
                                  (M ′ ∪Y M ) ∪ (M ∪Y N ) × {1}
                                                         

along the two copies of M , to obtain a bordism over ξG , witnessing the fact that (8.2) is equal
to [M ′ ∪Y N, ν M ′ ∪ −ν N ]. As the bordism class in (8.2) is trivial, we have that N is stably
diffeomorphic rel. Y to M ′ by Theorem 2.4. It follows that FY (M ) = {M, M ′ }, which completes
the proof.                                                                                     □
    Now we show, as promised, that whenever we have a pair of stably exotic fillings for a 3-
manifold Y , we can find infinitely many stable homeomorphism classes of pairs of stably exotic
fillings.
Proposition 8.3. Let M and M ′ be stably exotic fillings of Y . Then for all k ≥ 0,
                             Mk := M #k(S 1 × S 3 ) and Mk′ := M ′ #k(S 1 × S 3 )
are also stably exotic fillings of Y . Thus there are infinitely many stable homeomorphism classes
of fillings of Y , each of which contains a stably exotic pair.
16             DANIEL KASPROWSKI, PATRICK ORSON, MARK POWELL, AND ARUNIMA RAY


Proof. Since M and M ′ are stably homeomorphic rel. Y , so are Mk and Mk′ .
   Let H := π1 (M ) and let ξH : BH → BO be the normal 1-type of M and M ′ , with normal
1-type data (H, x, y). Let Fk denote the free group on k letters and let G := H ∗ Fk . Note that
H 1 (G; Z/2) ∼
             = H 1 (H; Z/2) ⊕ (Z/2)k and H 2 (G; Z/2) ∼ = H 2 (H; Z/2). Under these identifications
let w := (x, 0) ∈ H (G; Z/2) and let v := y ∈ H (G; Z/2). Since #k (S 1 × S 3 ) is spin, the normal
                    1                             2

1-type data of Mk and Mk′ is (G, w, v). Let ϕ : G → H be the projection. By Proposition 4.2, there
exists a map ϕB : BG → BH covering IdBO ×ϕ : BO ×K(G, 1) → BO ×K(H, 1) up to homotopy.
This map induces
                                    (ϕB )∗ : Ω4 (ξG ) → Ω4 (ξH ).
To show Mk and Mk′ are not stably diffeomorphic rel. Y , consider the union
                                     [Mk ∪Y Mk′ , ν Mk ∪ −ν Mk′ ] ∈ Ω4 (ξG )
for arbitrary normal 1-smoothings ν Mk and ν Mk′ that agree on Y . By Theorem 2.4, we need to
show that this is nontrivial. It suffices to show that its image
                               [Mk ∪Y Mk′ , ϕB ◦ ν Mk ∪ −ϕB ◦ ν Mk′ ] ∈ Ω4 (ξH ).                                (8.4)
under (ϕB )∗ is nontrivial.
   We claim that for each S 1 × S 3 summand, S 1 × S 3 = ∂(S 1 × D4 ) gives a ξH null-bordism of
[S × S 3 , ϕB ◦ ν Mk |S 1 ×S 3 ]. To see this, consider the map of fibrations:
  1


                        BSpin                  BO                 K(Z/2, 1) × K(Z/2, 2)
                                                                                 =

                         BH             BO ×K(H, 1)               K(Z/2, 1) × K(Z/2, 2).

Since the S 1 × S 3 summand maps trivially to K(H, 1), and is spin, the restriction of ϕB ◦ ν Mk to
S 1 × S 3 lifts to BSpin. Noting that S 1 × D4 is a spin filling, for either choice of spin structure on
S 1 × S 3 , it follows that S 1 × S 3 is null-bordant over BH as claimed.
   It follows from the claim that Mk is bordant rel. Y to M over ξH , for some normal 1-smoothing
ν M : M → BH . Similarly, Mk′ is bordant rel. Y to M ′ over ξH , for some normal 1-smoothing
ν M ′ : M ′ → BH . Moreover, by construction, (8.4) equals
                                      [M ∪Y M ′ , ν M ∪ −ν M ′ ] ∈ Ω4 (ξH ).
   Since M and M ′ are not stably diffeomorphic rel. Y , Theorem 2.4 implies that the latter union
is nontrivial in Ω4 (ξH ), as desired.                                                           □
